extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; scholars of Schopenhauer
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative criteria from Schopenhauer's Fourth Book on ethics: accounts of what constitutes good, bad, justice, virtue, conscience, revenge, love/charity, and their origins in relation to the will. Focuses on moral qualities as grounded in the metaphysics of the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good (relative) as relation to a will's ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything that furthers the ends desired by a will is called 'good' in a relative sense; men who are favourable to others' ends—who further and befriend them—are called good (helpful, benevolent, friendly, charitable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer emphasizes the relational nature of 'good' (των πρως τι); every good is essentially relative to a desiring will. The term 'good' for conscious beings carries the additional connotation of persistent helpful conduct toward the will of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute good (summum bonum) as denial of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute good is a contradiction except insofar as it is taken metaphorically to mean the complete self‑effacement and denial of the will—the true absence of will, which alone could for ever still and silence its struggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer argues there is no attainable permanent fulfilment of the will; the only radical cure is total resignation/denial of the will (ascetic ideal). The usual idea of a lasting summum bonum is unthinkable within the world's dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad (egoistic assertion of will)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is 'bad' if always disposed to do wrong when able—i.e., he asserts his own will so far as to deny the will appearing in other individuals, desiring their powers for his ends and seeking to destroy their existence when they obstruct him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This moral failure stems from excessive egoism and an intense vehemence of will combined with knowledge bound by the principium individuationis; such individuals treat others as mere masks and are indifferent to their suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wickedness/cruelty as disinterested delight in others' suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Wickedness proper arises when the suffering of others becomes an end in itself—not merely a means to one's own ends—manifesting as delight in others' pain and pure cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct from plain egoism, cruelty presupposes an inner misery from intense volition; Schopenhauer cites historical examples (Nero, Robespierre) and locates envy and the comparison of actual vs possible satisfaction of the will as psychological sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenge as disinterested recompense vs. punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Revenge recompenses evil with evil as an end in itself, for the past rather than the future; it is disinterested and revels in the torment inflicted. When identical acts are done according to established law in a sanctioned society, they become punishment (justice) rather than revenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer distinguishes revenge from legal punishment by intention and social sanction: revenge lacks the forward‑looking, rule‑based purpose of punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sting of conscience / remorse as metaphysical and volitional knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Remorse stems from two intimately united recognitions: (1) the illusiveness of the principium individuationis and the consequent unity of will in all, and (2) the self‑knowledge of the intensity with which one's will asserted itself to the detriment of others; together these produce the inward horror and lasting pain of conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remorse persists because the intelligible character feels itself free from time; past acts remain present to conscience. Suicide cannot escape this because what one wills inwardly one must be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good conscience as verification of direct knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction after a disinterested deed (good conscience) arises because such deeds verify the direct intuitive knowledge that one's true self exists in others; this enlarges the heart and yields serenity by diminishing anxious self‑interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good conscience results from deeds that flow from inner recognition (not from dogma) and produces evenness of disposition by extending concern beyond the singular self.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as the negation of the bad (voluntary respect for others' wills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the intermediate grade between bad and good: one who voluntarily recognizes and observes moral limits—who will not deny the will appearing in others and refrains from inflicting suffering or committing crime—is just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This voluntary observance holds even when not secured by external power; justice implies setting the external being on a level with oneself and includes respecting rights and property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher goodness / benevolence as deeper penetration of the principium individuationis
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond justice, a higher degree of penetration of the principium individuationis produces benevolence and disinterested love (caritas), where one makes less distinction between self and others and may sacrifice one's own well‑being or life for many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include heroes who die for others (Leonidas, Socrates); such goodness may coexist with a strong will yet be governed by knowledge that restrains blind striving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of genuine virtue: direct intuitive knowledge, not abstract dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine goodness and virtue do not arise from abstract moral theory or dogmas, because such knowledge provides only motives that can change the expression of the will but not the will itself (Velle non discitur). True virtue springs from direct intuitive recognition of others' inner nature as one's own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dogmas and preaching can influence outward conduct but cannot alter disposition; a virtuous disposition must be cultivated by immediate, noncommunicable insight and appears in actions rather than in verbal formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral worth depends on disposition, not mere outward acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward deeds (opera operata) are empty forms without moral significance unless they spring from a non‑egoistic disposition; identical outward acts can express the same inner disposition or very different ones, so moral judgment must attend to underlying motive and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer notes that equal degrees of wickedness can take very different external shapes across individuals or societies (e.g., murder vs. court intrigue); excessive external conformity (e.g., obedience to a doctrine) can produce no moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascetic renunciation as extreme form of justice/goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: When the penetration of individuation leads so far that a person doubts any right to inherited property, supports himself only by his own labour, and embraces voluntary poverty, this exceeds justice and becomes renunciation—the denial of the will to live (asceticism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer cites Pascal and certain Hindus as examples; he also warns of misunderstanding—some rich individuals may legitimately render services that justify their possessions, so extreme renunciation must be distinguished from mere scruple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love (agape/caritas) as sympathy: mitigation of others' suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure love (αγαπη, caritas) is essentially sympathy: since every wish proceeds from suffering, what goodness does for others is the alleviation of suffering; pure love is the direct knowledge of others' suffering set on a level with one's own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence works of love are motivated by the knowledge of others' suffering, not by abstract duty; sympathy is the operative standard by which charitable acts are morally grounded.
